newsitem.title: PERU: Peru weighs letting hostage takers leave country.
newsitem.headline: Peru weighs letting hostage takers leave country.

text.p: The Peruvian government said on Thursday it may allow Marxist rebels holding 74 captives at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima to leave the country if the hostage crisis ends peacefully.

"In a timely manner, we will announce to the press which countries would be disposed to receive these men," Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi told reporters, adding that for now any such contacts would remain secret.
He was responding to a question about whether Peru had been in touch with any foreign government about taking in the rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
"It is of course being considered," Pandolfi added.

President Alberto Fujimori has stuck to his tough line against the rebels, lambasting them as "terrorists" bent on pointless violence, but has said he will not consider storming the residence so long as none of the hostages is harmed.
Fujimori has said a "commission of guarantors" may be set up to oversee a peaceful solution to the crisis.
Earlier on Thursday, the rebels, who took over the compound on Dec. 17 to demand the release of about 400 jailed MRTA members, accused Fujimori of lying by saying they also want ransom money.
The rebels put a sign to a window at the besieged residence that read: "Do not lie Mr. Fujimori. Money does not interest us. The demand is freedom of our prisoners."

Fujimori's government had urged Japanese companies with employees being held hostage not to give in to rebel "blackmail." Although the MRTA has in the past kidnapped businessmen and politicians to raise money, there was no confirmation that that was their aim in the 23-day-old siege.
In another sign at the window, the guerrillas said they had explained why they were still holding about two dozen Japanese captives to a reporter and a translator from Japan's TV Asahi.
Police arrested the two men on Tuesday after they sneaked past security officers for a two-hour meeting with the rebels.
Pandolfi said the two would be released but that their film and notebooks would be confiscated.
A TV Asahi official said the company still wanted the journalists' material returned.

The rebels have freed most of the more than 500 hostages they originally took upon storming the residence during a cocktail party, but say no more will be let out until the government's chief negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, meets them again inside the residence.
Fujimori, who has vowed not to release the jailed rebels, said on Wednesday he was waiting for "favorable conditions" before sending Palermo back to the mined and booby-trapped compound.
Talks between the government and rebels stopped abruptly after a first face-to-face meeting 12 days ago between Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini inside the residence.
Fujimori has said the talks were stalled by an impromptu news conference by the guerrillas on New Year's Eve that he said derailed concessions the two sides had hammered out.

The MRTA responded to Palermo's first meeting by freeing 20 captives. A steady trickle of releases dried up on Jan. 1 with the rebels still holding top government and security force officials, Japanese businessmen and diplomats and Fujimori's brother Pedro.
Pandolfi also denied a newspaper report which said that the chief security adviser to Fujimori had met with several jailed leaders of the MRTA.
"I can affirm that Dr. Vladimiro Montesinos does not even know the prison" in question, Pandolfi said.

Citing unnamed military sources, opposition daily La Republica said on Thursday that Montesinos had visited MRTA leaders Victor Polay Campos and Miguel Rincon Rincon in recent weeks and offered the hostage-takers safe passage to leave Peru if they surrendered their arms and freed the last hostages.
Montesinos, a controversial figure seldom seen in public, is widely considered to be Fujimori's right-hand man and has spent much of the crisis holed up with the president planning strategy.
